title: McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y
blurb: Explain Theory X and Theory Y as a manager's assumptions about people, show how those assumptions become self-fulfilling, and choose the approach that gets the best from a project team.
question: An insurance company's project manager believes developers 'slack off' when working from home, so he demands hourly updates and approves every code change himself. The developers now wait for his sign-off instead of solving problems, and he says this proves they can't be trusted. Using McGregor, explain what is happening and what he should do instead.

teach.body: McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y describe two sets of ASSUMPTIONS a manager can hold about people at work. A Theory X manager assumes people dislike work and need control and direction. A Theory Y manager assumes people seek responsibility and are self-motivated, given the right conditions. In plain English: what you believe about your team shapes how you lead it, and how you lead it shapes how the team behaves.

This is the heart of McGregor. A Theory X manager supervises closely, so people stop using initiative and wait to be told. The manager sees that as proof they need control, and tightens it further. A Theory Y manager gives trust and responsibility, so people take ownership and use their judgement, which confirms the manager's belief. Either way, the manager's behaviour helps create the very behaviour they expected.

Dan assumes his developers will slack when working from home, so he demands hourly updates and approves every pull request. They stop proposing improvements and queue for his sign-off; throughput drops, and Dan feels proved right. His replacement, Mo, agrees sprint goals with the team, lets them self-organise and reviews outcomes at each sprint review. Ownership returns and throughput rises: the same people, different assumptions.

teach.h: Is Theory X behaviour ever right?
teach.body: McGregor argued Theory Y assumptions get more from most people, especially in knowledge work. But firm direction is sometimes needed: an emergency, a safety-critical procedure, or someone brand new to a task. Choosing directive behaviour for a situation is not the same as holding Theory X beliefs. A Theory Y leader can give clear instructions in a crisis and still trust people the rest of the time.

teach.text: The classic trap: Theory X and Theory Y describe the MANAGER'S assumptions about people, not two types of worker. Theory Y is not 'no leadership': it still sets clear goals and tolerances, it just trusts people to find the way. And don't mix McGregor (X and Y) with Herzberg (hygiene factors and motivators).

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Define both: Theory X assumes people dislike work and need control; Theory Y assumes they seek responsibility and self-motivate in the right conditions.
Explain the self-fulfilling effect: the leader's behaviour produces the behaviour the assumption predicts.
Diagnose the scenario: which assumption is the PM acting on, and what is it doing to ownership and openness?
Recommend Theory Y practice: shared goals, involvement, delegation within tolerances, outcome-based review.
Add judgement: directive behaviour can still be right in a crisis or for a novice, without Theory X beliefs.
Theory X and Y are a manager's assumptions about people, not types of people.
Theory X: people dislike work and need control and direction.
Theory Y: people seek responsibility and are self-motivated in the right conditions.
The assumptions become self-fulfilling through the way the manager leads.
Iterative, self-organising teams depend on Theory Y; directive behaviour in a crisis is a situational choice.

summary: You can now explain Theory X and Theory Y as a manager's assumptions about people and show how they become self-fulfilling. You can also recommend Theory Y practices for linear, iterative and hybrid teams while recognising when firm direction is still needed.

A.q: McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y are BEST described as:
options: A manager's assumptions about what motivates people
Two personality types found in every project team
Two stages a team passes through as it matures
Factors that cause satisfaction or dissatisfaction
A.why: Theory X and Theory Y are two contrasting sets of assumptions a manager may hold about people at work, which shape how they lead.

whyNot.1: They describe managers' beliefs about people, not personality types.
whyNot.2: Team development stages come from Tuckman, not McGregor.
whyNot.3: Satisfaction and dissatisfaction factors are Herzberg's two-factor theory.

A.q: A Theory Y manager assumes that people:
options: dislike work and must be closely supervised
are motivated mainly by fear of punishment
will seek responsibility in the right conditions
prefer to be directed and to avoid responsibility
A.why: Theory Y assumes people are self-motivated and will seek responsibility when the conditions are right.

whyNot.0: This is a Theory X assumption.
whyNot.1: Fear of punishment as the main motivator is a Theory X assumption.
whyNot.3: Preferring direction and avoiding responsibility is a Theory X assumption.

A.q: Which leadership behaviour is MOST typical of a Theory X manager?
options: Agreeing goals and letting the team plan the work
Checking every task and approving all decisions
Inviting the team to suggest process improvements
Delegating work packages within clear tolerances
A.why: Close supervision and central control follow from the Theory X belief that people need direction to perform.

whyNot.0: Shared goals with team-led planning reflect Theory Y trust.
whyNot.2: Inviting improvement ideas assumes people want to contribute: Theory Y.
whyNot.3: Delegating within tolerances trusts people to deliver: Theory Y.

B.q: What does it mean to say McGregor's assumptions are 'self-fulfilling'?
options: People always fulfil the targets their manager sets
Theory Y managers fulfil their own needs before others
Teams move from Theory X to Theory Y as they mature
Behaviour shaped by the assumption ends up proving it
B.why: The way a manager leads, based on their assumption, draws out behaviour that seems to confirm the assumption.

whyNot.0: Self-fulfilling refers to assumptions shaping behaviour, not hitting targets.
whyNot.1: This confuses McGregor with ideas about personal needs (closer to Maslow).
whyNot.2: X and Y are manager assumptions, not stages teams pass through.

B.q: A PM leading a hybrid team insists cameras stay on all day and asks for hourly updates because 'people slack off at home'. Which assumption does this reflect?
options: Theory X
Theory Y
Herzberg's motivators
Maslow's esteem needs
B.why: Assuming people avoid work unless watched, and controlling them closely, is classic Theory X.

whyNot.1: Theory Y would trust the team and manage by outputs.
whyNot.2: Herzberg's motivators (achievement, responsibility) are about what motivates, not distrustful control.
whyNot.3: Esteem needs relate to recognition and respect; close monitoring tends to undermine them.

B.q: Which statement about Theory X and Theory Y is correct?
options: Theory Y means removing all goals and structure
Theory X describes lazy workers, not managers
Directive behaviour can be used without X beliefs
McGregor argued Theory X suits most knowledge work
B.why: A leader may choose firm direction for a situation such as an emergency without believing people are lazy. That is a situational choice, not Theory X.

whyNot.0: Theory Y still sets clear goals; it trusts people with how to reach them.
whyNot.1: Theory X describes a manager's assumptions about workers, not a type of worker.
whyNot.3: McGregor favoured Theory Y assumptions as the more effective basis for managing most people.

C.q: A software company's PM approves every code change personally. Developers now wait for his sign-off instead of solving problems, and he concludes they 'can't be trusted'. What is the BEST explanation?
options: The developers are in Tuckman's storming stage
His Theory X approach has created the behaviour
The developers' hygiene factors have been removed
He is correctly applying a Theory Y style to them
C.why: His controlling behaviour, based on Theory X assumptions, has removed initiative, and he reads the result as proof: a self-fulfilling prophecy.

whyNot.0: Storming is about conflict and challenge; here the developers have become passive.
whyNot.2: Nothing suggests pay, conditions or policies have changed.
whyNot.3: Approving every change and distrusting the team is the opposite of Theory Y.

C.q:
An iterative team is expected to self-organise around each sprint goal. Which TWO assumptions underpin this?
1. People can direct their own work towards agreed goals
2. People need close supervision to perform
3. People avoid responsibility wherever possible
4. People can use creativity to solve problems
options: 1 and 2
2 and 3
3 and 4
1 and 4
C.why: Self-organisation rests on Theory Y assumptions: self-direction towards goals (1) and creative problem-solving (4).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is a Theory X assumption that conflicts with self-organisation.
whyNot.1: Both 2 and 3 are Theory X assumptions.
whyNot.2: Statement 3 is a Theory X assumption.

C.q: A PM on a linear construction project with experienced site teams wants to apply Theory Y while keeping control. Which approach is MOST appropriate?
options: Delegate work packages with clear goals and tolerances
Inspect every activity daily against the detailed plan
Remove the plan so teams can decide what to deliver
Hold back information so teams focus on their tasks
C.why: Delegating with clear goals and tolerances trusts experienced people (Theory Y) while the PM keeps control through the plan and exception reporting.

whyNot.1: Daily inspection of every activity is Theory X control.
whyNot.2: Theory Y doesn't remove goals or plans; it trusts people with how to meet them.
whyNot.3: Withholding information signals distrust and reduces ownership.

reteach.title: Think of two parents and the homework
reteach.question: Two parents help their teenagers with homework. One sits beside them checking every line; the other agrees what is due and trusts them to get on with it. A term later, which teenager takes more responsibility, and why?

blocks.h: The parents' beliefs shape the teenagers
blocks.body: Parent X believes the teenager won't work unless watched, so checks every line. The teenager stops trying to get it right first time and waits for corrections. Parent X concludes: 'See, I have to check everything.' Parent Y believes the teenager can manage, agrees the deadline and is available for help. The teenager learns to plan and owns the result. Each parent's belief created the behaviour they expected.

blocks.text: Theory X and Y describe the PARENT (the manager), not the teenager (the team member). Change the assumption and the behaviour usually follows.

explain.body: A Theory X manager assumes people dislike work, avoid responsibility and need control and direction. The style that follows is directive: close supervision, detailed rules and checks, and reward or sanction to drive effort.

test.q: Which is a Theory X assumption about people at work?
options: They find work as natural as rest or play
They seek responsibility given the chance
They need direction and control to perform
They are creative problem-solvers by nature
test.why: Theory X assumes people need direction and control because they dislike work.

whyNot.0: Seeing work as natural is a Theory Y assumption.
whyNot.1: Seeking responsibility is a Theory Y assumption.
whyNot.3: Creativity and problem-solving are Theory Y assumptions.

explain.body: A Theory Y manager assumes people find work natural, seek responsibility and are self-motivated when the conditions are right. The style that follows is participative: agree goals, involve people, delegate and review outcomes rather than activity.

test.q: Which management practice BEST reflects Theory Y?
options: Using sanctions to keep output on track
Agreeing objectives and trusting the team
Logging each person's hours to the minute
Approving every decision centrally
test.why: Agreeing objectives and trusting people to meet them reflects Theory Y's belief in self-direction and responsibility.

whyNot.0: Sanctions to drive output reflect Theory X.
whyNot.2: Minute-by-minute tracking reflects Theory X distrust.
whyNot.3: Centralised approval of every decision reflects Theory X control.

explain.body: Whatever the manager assumes tends to come true, because the manager's behaviour shapes the team's. Control breeds passivity, which 'proves' control was needed. Trust breeds ownership, which 'proves' trust was deserved.

test.q: A PM believes the team is unmotivated, so gives them only simple, closely checked tasks. Over time the team shows less initiative. What has MOST likely happened?
options: The team has reached Maslow's self-actualisation
The PM has applied Herzberg's motivators well
The team has been given too much responsibility
The PM's assumption has become self-fulfilling
test.why: Treating people as unmotivated removed their chances to show initiative, so the PM's belief appears confirmed.

whyNot.0: Simple, closely checked tasks block growth rather than enabling self-actualisation.
whyNot.1: Herzberg's motivators include responsibility and the work itself, which the PM has removed.
whyNot.2: They were given less responsibility, not more.

explain.body: Hold Theory Y assumptions by default, but choose behaviour to fit the situation. In an emergency, a safety-critical step or with someone new to a task, firm direction is right. That is a situational choice, not a belief that people are lazy.

test.q: During a site safety emergency, a normally participative PM gives firm, direct instructions. What does this show?
options: A situational choice, not a Theory X belief
The PM has switched to Theory X permanently
Theory Y managers must never give instructions
The team has fallen back to the forming stage
test.why: Firm direction in an emergency is a choice of behaviour to suit the situation. It doesn't mean the PM now distrusts the team.

whyNot.1: One crisis response doesn't change the PM's underlying assumptions.
whyNot.2: Theory Y managers give direction when the situation demands it.
whyNot.3: An emergency calls for direction whatever the team's stage of development.
